catalog_quote: 1. PHONOLOGICAL WORD In Mixtepec Mixtec the minimal phonological word is made up of the sequence of two syllables — a couplet. This couplet is the complex nucleus of the word; the first syllable is marked phonologically by a lengthened vowel unless that vowel is preceding /?/ [scan of /ʔ/] ... 'you (pl. fam.) are going to sell again'. Loudness, stress, usually occurs on the first syllable of the couplet. When, however, tone 1 or tone 2 precedes tone 3, the syllable preceding the tone 3 may be louder than the first syllable: villu1-yu3 'my (polite) cat', ei3so2-yu3 'my (polite) brother-in-law'. The loudness is especially noticeable on the tone clusters 1-3 and 2-3: villu1-3 'my (fam.) cat', ei3so2-3 'my (fam.) brother-in-law'.

new_statements.quote: In Mixtepec (Mix) (E. V. Pike & Ibach 1978:271–272), the first vowel of the couplet is usually louder than other vowels, and in couplets that do not have a couplet-medial glottal stop, the first vowel of the couplet has longer duration than other vowels. [p. 86] ... Similar stress systems are described for the Mixtec varieties from Molinos ..., Huajuapan ..., and Mixtepec (Mix) (E. V. Pike & Ibach 1978:272). ... However, in two varieties (Ayutla and Mixtepec) where lengthening of the first vowel of the couplet is also mentioned, the tone-dependent stress is distinguished from that lengthening. The lengthening of the couplet is not influenced by tone sequence, while the tone-dependent stress is associated with loudness. [pp. 92-93]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Three-tone language. According to Pike & Ibach 1978 as relayed by Carroll: the first vowel of the bimoraic root ('couplet') is regularly the most prominent (louder; lengthened unless a glottal stop follows it), i.e. couplet-initial prominence independent of tone; in addition Pike & Ibach report an Ayutla-style tone-conditioned 'stress' (attracted to the first syllable of a falling-tone sequence within couplet+enclitics, defaulting to the couplet-initial syllable), which they keep distinct from the couplet-initial lengthening. Later authors (Hyman 2006, McKendry 2013, Carroll 2015) read such systems as fixed couplet-initial stress with the tone-dependent effect being perceptual.
new_statements.exceptions: Lengthening of the couplet-initial vowel is suspended when a couplet-medial glottal stop follows; tone-dependent stress may fall on post-couplet enclitic syllables (by analogy with Ayutla; Carroll gives no Mixtepec examples). Bowers 2020 notes Spanish loans map Spanish stress to H tone + length.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the couplet (bimoraic root, CVCV or CVV) plus enclitics for the tone-dependent effect; prefixes are outside the stressable domain. Statement is second-hand: Carroll paraphrases Pike & Ibach 1978:271-272 (San Juan Mixtepec town dialect, SIL fieldwork). The modern first-hand sketches of the Yucunani dialect (Paster & Beam de Azcona 2004; Bowers 2020) are silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Two sub-varieties are involved, both under mixt1425 / ISO mix: Pike & Ibach 1978 describe the San Juan Mixtepec town dialect; Paster & Beam de Azcona 2004, Paster 2010, Bowers 2020 and the UCSB Salazar/Belmar/Campbell papers describe the Yucunani (Yucunany, Sa'an Savi na Yukunani) village dialect of the same municipio. Carroll 2015, the work quoted, is itself a description of Ixpantepec Nieves Mixtec, which Glottolog files under Silacayoapan Mixtec [mks], not [mix]; only its literature-review paraphrase of Pike & Ibach concerns mixt1425.

tone_statements.citation: Belmar Viernes, Guillem. 2024. Community-informed documentary linguistics and community-led participatory research: describing Sà'án Sàvǐ ñà ñuù Xnúvíkó and analyzing speakers' insights on intelligibility with Tlahuapa Mixtec. PhD dissertation, University of California, Santa Barbara. eScholarship qt1sp7r83c.
tone_statements.quote: The Tone Bearing Unit (TBU) is the mora. In Sà'án Sàvǐ ñà ñuù Xnúvíkó each mora hosts one of six phonological tones. These are divided into four level tones: high (H), mid (M), low-mid (m), low (L);32 and two contour tones: rising (R) and falling (F). These tones are combined to form melodies, which may then be modified to mark grammatical information. ... In this analysis, the contour tones are treated as tones in their own right, rather than combinations of level tones.
tone_statements.summary: Six tones per mora (H, M, low-mid, L; unit rising and falling); 23 melodies on disyllabic, 19 on monosyllabic bimoraic nouns; little sandhi (R>H in compounds); grammatical tone; root-final stress.

Tonal alternation A Rising tone in the first mora indicates negation (16) Ñà-ka kúu-ñà ntsìnì-yù ... ntsìnì=yù ... PFV.see=1 'This is what I have seen' (17) Cha ntsǐnì sò'o tuku-kue-tù ... ntsǐnì-sò'o ... NEG.PFV.see-ear ... 'And we also didn't understand it!'
tone_statements.summary: 4 level tones plus 'several' contour tones (no total given); grammatical tone: a rising tone on the verb's first mora marks negation (sl. 17-18); 1sg glossed as a bare L enclitic (=ᴸ).

tone_statements.citation: Auderset, Sandra. 2022. Supplementary Material: Standardization of tone notations. 'Rates of change and phylogenetic signal in Mixtec tone'. Leipzig: Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology / University of California Santa Barbara, 15 August 2022. 24 pp. Distributed as in the Mixtecan Cognate Database (MixteCoDB, github.com/SAuderset/MixteCoDB, CC BY-SA 4.0) and as definitions/ in MixteCaSo (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.10143870).
tone_statements.quote: San Juan Mixtepec Mixtec. The data for this variety comes from two sources: Josserand (1983) and Dürr (1987). There are three levels tones (low, mid, high) and two contours (rising and falling) combining into 14 distinct tone melodies in our data. The level tones can appear on either mora and combine with each other freely. The rising contour tone can appear on either mora as well. The rare falling tone seems to be restricted to the first mora. [p. 12] ... Yucunani Mixtec. The data for this variety was shared by collaborator and native speaker Jeremías Salazar. The orthography used is latin-based ? and tones are marked throughout with diacritics (MULG). There are three levels tones (low, mid, high) and two contours (rising and falling) combining into 15 distinct tone melodies in our data. [p. 13]
tone_statements.locator: p. 12 'San Juan Mixtepec Mixtec' and p. 13 'Yucunani Mixtec' (section Group 7 > Group 71)
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones (L, M, H) plus rising and falling contour tones, mora as TBU, 14-16 contrastive melodies on bimoraic couplets; *H > M, *L > L, glottal-stop loss yields H or HL.

tone_statements.quote: The dialects Mixtepec, Alacatlazala and Metlatonoc mostly show reflexes of *high-highˀ and *low-lowˀ having a final high tone or tone rising to high. ... [Chart 3, Mixtepec rows] *HIGH-HIGHˀ: CVCV: fml-rlh, CVˀV: mid-high | *HIGH-HIGH: mid-mid | *HIGH-LOW: mid-low (fml-mid) | *LOW-HIGH: low-mid (rlm-low) | *LOW-LOWˀ: CVCV: low-rlh, CVV: low-high | *LOW-LOW: low-low ... sources.quote: The dialects Mixtepec, Alacatlazala and Metlatonoc mostly show reflexes of *high-highˀ and *low-lowˀ having a final high tone or tone rising to high. ... [Chart 3, Mixtepec rows] *HIGH-HIGHˀ: CVCV: fml-rlh, CVˀV: mid-high | *HIGH-HIGH: mid-mid | *HIGH-LOW: mid-low (fml-mid) | *LOW-HIGH: low-mid (rlm-low) | *LOW-LOWˀ: CVCV: low-rlh, CVV: low-high | *LOW-LOW: low-low ... Tonal glides: h high tone m mid tone l low tone r rising f falling rlh glide rising from low to high fml glide falling from mid to low
sources.note: Comparative work: gives Mixtepec (Pike & Ibach 1978 data) tonemic couplets with high, mid, low and glides fml/rlh/rlm; no tone count for Mixtepec. Note 12: sandhi HH>LH after low.

sources.note: Article describes a tone-change module: 'Out of the 105 varieties for which segmental changes can be annotated, only 46 have tones marked on more than a few entries'; tone values are standardized per source and coded per cognate.
